scenarios.title: Scenario 5 — Claude Code for Continuous Integration
scenarios.brief: A travel-booking company runs Claude Code in GitHub Actions on a Kotlin and TypeScript repository. It has four jobs: a pull-request review that posts inline comments, an autofix job for failing builds, test generation for new endpoints, and a weekly dependency-risk report. The review job uses an MCP server for code search and API guidelines. CLAUDE.md and .claude/ are committed.

scenarios.title: Scenario 2 — Code Generation with Claude Code
scenarios.brief: A startup uses Claude Code in one TypeScript repository with server/, mobile/ and packages/shared/ folders. The repository commits a .claude/ directory and a root CLAUDE.md. Engineers use Claude Code to generate endpoints, screens and tests from tickets.

scenarios.title: Scenario 4 — Developer Productivity with Claude
scenarios.brief: A language-learning company's platform team uses Claude Code on a large Ruby on Rails app with a React front end. Engineers read and change code with the built-in tools: Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep and Glob. MCP servers connect Claude to Linear and a staging Postgres database. Some engineers also script Claude with the Agent SDK for internal tools.

questions.question: A developer added a line to the committed root CLAUDE.md. It says: “Explain every change in detail, I am new to Kotlin.” Now the CI review job posts long teaching comments on every pull request. Teammates' own sessions have started explaining everything too. The developer still wants detailed answers in all of their own sessions. Where should the line live?

options.t: In a .claude/rules/ file whose paths: glob matches only the Kotlin files.
options.why: Works, but still shared. The rule is committed, so CI and teammates load it whenever a Kotlin file is touched, which is most of the time.

options.t: In the developer's own ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, removed from the committed project file.
options.why: Best. User-level memory is personal and not shared through git. It loads in every one of the developer's sessions, in every project, and nobody else's.

options.t: In a project skill that the developer invokes at the start of each of their sessions.
options.why: Works, but only when remembered. It is also committed, so the skill shows up for the whole team.

options.t: In the CI job's -p prompt, as an override asking for short review comments.
options.why: Works, but for CI only. The review gets shorter, yet teammates' sessions still load the line from the root file.

questions.decider: The developer still wants detailed answers in all of their own sessions.
questions.explanation: A personal preference belongs in user-level ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md. It is not shared through version control, so it changes only that person's sessions.

eli5.question: One developer's personal wish (“explain everything to me”) went into the shared file. Now CI and teammates get it too.
eli5.answer: A sticky note on the office noticeboard is read by everyone. A note in your own notebook is read only by you, wherever you go. The root CLAUDE.md is the noticeboard; ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md is your notebook. Rule: only for me → user-level memory. For the team → the project file.
options: A note that pops up on Kotlin files is still on the noticeboard: CI and teammates see it.
Correct. Your own notebook: you get it everywhere, and nobody else does.
A note you must remember to fetch each morning, and the whole team can see it.
Telling CI to ignore it helps CI, but teammates still read the noticeboard.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think the problem is CI's output, so the fix goes in CI. The real fault is the home of the line: a personal wish sits in a file that every clone and every CI run loads. Move it to the file that only this person loads.

~/.claude/CLAUDE.md  → this developer, every project
repo/CLAUDE.md       → every teammate and every CI run

questions.question: An engineer wrote a /new-screen command that creates a screen, its test and its story in the team's layout. It lives in their ~/.claude/commands/. Teammates copied it from a chat message, and the copies have drifted, so new screens come out in different layouts. The team wants one version that every engineer gets with the code. Where should the command live?

options.t: In the repository's .claude/commands/ folder, committed alongside the code.
options.why: Best. Project commands live in the repository, so every engineer gets the same version on clone or pull, and changes go through review.

options.t: In the root CLAUDE.md, as a section that lists the steps for a new screen.
options.why: Works, but wrong kind of file. Claude can follow the steps, but they load into every session and there is no /new-screen to run.

options.t: In a .claude/rules/ file whose paths: glob matches *.screen.tsx.
options.why: Works, but loads too late. A path rule loads when a matching file is touched, and the screen does not exist until the command creates it.

options.t: In a team dotfiles repo that copies it into each engineer's ~/.claude/commands/.
options.why: Works, but outside the project. Each engineer must install and update the dotfiles, so versions can drift again.

questions.decider: The team wants one version that every engineer gets with the code.
questions.explanation: A command the whole team should share lives in the project's .claude/commands/, committed to git. ~/.claude/commands/ is for personal commands.

eli5.question: A handy command lives on one person's laptop. Everyone copied it, and the copies no longer match.
eli5.answer: If the whole crew needs the same tool, leave it in the shared toolshed on site, not in one person's van. The repository's .claude/commands/ is the shared toolshed: whoever clones gets the same tool, and any change is reviewed. Rule: a team command → .claude/commands/ in the repo. A personal command → ~/.claude/commands/.
options: Correct. One tool in the shared toolshed; everyone gets the same one.
Written instructions on the wall aren't a tool you can pick up, and everyone reads them all day.
A note that appears only next to finished screens can't help you make a new one.
Copying the tool into every van works until someone forgets to update theirs.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think the drift is a sharing problem to solve with a sync tool. Claude Code already has a shared home for commands: the repository's .claude/commands/. Committed there, the command arrives with the code and changes go through review.

questions.question: The team's API style guide lives in docs/api-style.md, and the API team updates it often. The root CLAUDE.md holds a pasted copy of the guide. That copy is months out of date, so Claude follows rules the guide has since changed. The guide applies to every endpoint in the app. What is the best fix?

options.t: Replace the copy with an @import line naming the guide file in docs/.
options.why: Best. The import pulls the live guide into memory, so there is one copy to maintain and Claude always reads the current rules.

options.t: Add a CI step that copies the latest guide into CLAUDE.md after every merge.
options.why: Works, but overbuilt. It keeps the copy fresh with a moving part you must build and maintain, when an import line does it with no copy.

options.t: Move the guide into an /api-style skill that engineers invoke for endpoint work.
options.why: Works, but only when invoked. Endpoints written without the skill miss the guide, and the skill is another copy.

options.t: Paste the guide into a .claude/rules/ file with a paths: glob on the controllers.
options.why: Works, but still a copy. It loads more precisely, yet it drifts from docs/ exactly like the pasted copy did.

questions.decider: That copy is months out of date, so Claude follows rules the guide has since changed.
questions.explanation: @import lets CLAUDE.md reference a file instead of copying it, so memory stays in step with the source document.

eli5.question: The rule book was photocopied into Claude's notes. The real rule book changed; the photocopy didn't.
eli5.answer: Instead of a photocopy pinned to the wall, pin a note that says “read the rule book on shelf 3”. Whoever reads the note always gets the current book. An @import line in CLAUDE.md is that note. Rule: the content already lives in a file → import it, don't copy it.
options: Correct. Point at the real book, so there's nothing to keep in sync.
A machine that re-photocopies the book after every change works, but it's a machine to keep running.
Locking the book in a cupboard means people only read it when they remember to open the cupboard.
A neater photocopy in a better spot is still a photocopy that goes stale.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think this is about where the guide should load. The guide applies to every endpoint, so always-loaded memory is already the right place. The fault is that memory holds a copy. @import makes CLAUDE.md point at the source file instead.
